title: To learn to die
hookLine: Montaigne: to philosophize is to learn to die, and he'd like death to find him planting cabbages
last: A MIRROR OF THE TIME TO COME.

lines: A MAN AT A WRITING TABLE.
cards: A man sits at a writing table in France, working on short pieces that wander from quotation to gossip to confession and back. He is not a priest or a professor. He is a reader who wants to know how to live.
One piece takes its title from a line of Cicero's: that to philosophize is to learn to die. Michel de Montaigne writes it plainly, and somewhere in it he says how he would like death to find him.
Not in some grand last scene. Planting cabbages.

teach.h: TO PHILOSOPHIZE IS TO PREPARE FOR DEATH.
teach.b: First, the title. Montaigne opens by citing Cicero: to philosophize is nothing other than to prepare for death. He takes the line seriously, then makes it his own.
Second, the usual remedy, and his complaint.

Ordinary people, he says, deal with death by not thinking about it, and he calls that a kind of blindness: when it comes, to them or to someone they love, it lands with full force on someone unprepared.
His answer: take away death's strangeness. Spend time with it. Get used to it.

teach.h: LEARN TO DIE, UNLEARN BEING A SLAVE.
teach.b: Keep it in mind often, not to be gloomy, but so it stops being a stranger at the door. Third, why bother.
To think ahead about death, he says, is to think ahead about freedom: a person who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave.
Knowing how to die, he goes on, frees us from every kind of subjection and constraint. Loosen that one fear, and much else loosens. Fourth, the cabbages.
Here's the turn. He doesn't want to spend his life brooding.
He wants to be busy with ordinary work, and he'd like death to find him planting his cabbages, not caring about death, and caring even less about the garden left unfinished.

That's the week, too: five answers to suffering kept apart, Socrates's either way, Plato's practice of letting go, Lucretius's mirror, and now Montaigne, learning to die so that he can go on planting.

how: Some readers of Montaigne take his essay as an invitation to think about death calmly and often, not to dwell on it, but to loosen the fear and get on with ordinary life.

games.q: you are Montaigne, thinking about how you'd like death to find you. what do you choose?
o: in a great speech, with everyone listening.
planting cabbages, not caring about death or the unfinished garden.
with every task finished and every drawer in order.
games.why: he picks the ordinary: busy in the garden, unbothered by death, and less bothered still by what's left undone.

practice: This one is gentle, and you can skip it; if a loss is close right now, rest in the breath instead.

If you'd like, picture once, calmly, the plain fact that a day will come, no accident, no hospital drama, and hold it for a few breaths, the way you'd look at a stranger's face until it looks less strange.
Then let it go, and see yourself doing something ordinary that you love: your own cabbages.

wordCard.voice: Montaigne, who took Cicero's line that to philosophize is to learn to die, and hoped to be found planting his cabbages. Today's word.
